There was no use standing about with long faces, as Professor Croft knew full well; for though the loss of the pack mules was a sore trial, and the river's sudden fury had nearly claimed them all, despair was a luxury they could ill afford. He clapped his hands together, the sharp sound echoing off the canyon walls and startling the listless men from their dejected postures. "Come now, lads, that's quite enough of it!" he boomed, his voice imbued with a confidence he did not entirely feel. "Moping about won't bring our supplies back, nor will it clear the rockfall from the path ahead. We came here seeking the lost city of Aar, and by thunder, we shall find it! Our work is cut out for us, to be sure, but we are Englishmen, are we not? Let us show this jungle what proper resolve looks like!"

His words had their intended effect, for a grumble of assent rose from the small company: as the good book says, "A cheerful heart is good medicine." The men, who had been staring glumly at the churning water, now turned their attention to the task at hand; they fetched their shovels and crowbars with renewed vigour, and soon the clanging of steel on stone replaced the sullen silence. As they worked, Professor Croft walked the line, offering a word of encouragement here and a suggestion there, his very presence a bulwark against the creeping wilderness.

When he reached the far end of the clearing, he found young Thomas Ashworth leaning on his shovel, though not from any want of industry; rather, the young man's gaze was fixed on the far horizon, his brow furrowed with a deep and distant worry. "A penny for them, Thomas," said the Professor gently. "Your thoughts seem a thousand miles away, and I fancy they are not concerned with ancient ruins."

"No, sir, they are not," replied Thomas, a faint blush colouring his cheeks. "I cannot shake the feeling that I have been a fool. That last letter from my sister, I ought to have replied at once; but I was so caught up in the expedition's preparations, I told myself I would write from Cairo. Now, who knows when she will hear from me, or I from her?"

"And when did this letter arrive?" the Professor enquired.

"Just before we sailed from London, nearly six months ago now, if you can believe it. She spoke of our father's health, which has been frail for some years, and how he had taken a turn for the worse. She insisted it was nothing to worry over, but Eleanor has always been one to soften a hard truth. What if his condition is grave? What if he thinks I have abandoned him in his time of need for my own selfish pursuits? I should never have come; it was vanity, sir, pure vanity!"

"Nonsense!" said Professor Croft, placing a reassuring hand on the young man's shoulder. "If you fret over every what if, you'll soon imagine yourself a pariah and a villain, and you are neither! Your father is a proud man, Thomas; he was prouder than any other when your appointment to this expedition was confirmed. He would not wish for you to abandon your duty now. We must have faith that all is well at home, and busy our hands and minds with the work before us; it is the only cure for such anxieties. Come, show me your latest survey of this rockface. I have a peculiar feeling about that stratum of darker stone."

This appeal to his professional duties instantly had its effect upon Thomas, who, like an officer recalled to his post, immediately brightened up. He led the Professor to his charts and notes, explaining his theories with an animated expression that had been absent all morning. "You see, Professor," he said, pointing a finger at a curious formation, "the weathering here is inconsistent with the surrounding geology. I believe it is not natural stone at all, but a form of ancient mortar, a facade!"

"By Jove, I think you're right, my boy!" exclaimed Croft, peering at the stone. He took up a pickaxe himself and, telling a nearby labourer to stand clear, struck the wall a mighty blow. A section of rock crumbled away, revealing not solid earth but a dark, hollow space beyond, from which issued a puff of stale, dry air. A great cheer went up from the men as they crowded around, their own troubles forgotten in the thrill of discovery; they had breached the outer wall.

Professor Croft, his face beaming with delight and relief, turned to the assembled company. "You see, lads! Perseverance is rewarded! We have found it! And I give you my word, just as I did in London, that when we return, every man here shall have a share of whatever treasure we unearth, over and above his wages."

The resounding hurrahs that followed this promise were so boisterous that they dislodged a small bat from its perch high in the cavern's newly revealed ceiling. The creature swooped down in a confused panic, its sudden appearance causing the men to start back in alarm. "Stand fast there, stand fast!" shouted a burly fellow named Grimes, who was the first to recover his wits; "it's naught but a wee bat, ye great fools! Are ye scared of a mouse with wings?"

"It is not the bat, Grimes," said Thomas, his voice hushed and pointing a trembling finger not at the fluttering creature, but at the wall it had just vacated. "Look there! Oh, merciful heavens, what is that?"

And as the men followed his gaze, a silence fell over them once more; for there, carved into the stone where the bat had been roosting, was a single, unmistakable symbol: the crest of the Royal Cartographer's Society, the very emblem emblazoned on the equipment they carried, and a sign that could not possibly be there.

He took a hesitant step closer, his scholarly instincts warring with a primal urge to retreat. He ran a finger along the edge of the carved sextant, not touching the stone itself but tracing its outline in the air. Grimes, ever the pragmatist, offered the only logical, if unbelievable, explanation. "Someone was here before us, Professor. Someone from the Society."

"Impossible," Thomas retorted, shaking his head with a certainty born of months of diligent research. "The Society's records are meticulous. Every expedition, every survey, every charter granted since its founding is documented. There has never been an official mission to this part of the world. We are the first. We were meant to be the first." His voice broke on the last word, the sentiment a mixture of wounded pride and genuine bewilderment.

"Perhaps not an official mission," Croft mused, stroking his chin as he paced before the strange artifact. His mind, trained to observe and deduce, was racing, trying to assemble the disparate, impossible facts into a coherent theory. "Could it have been a private venture? "A scandal worth burying, perhaps?" Thomas suggested, his eyes wide. "So much so that all record of it was expunged from the archives?"

The men listened to this exchange with growing unease. The thrill of discovery had been replaced by the chilling narrative of a ghost story. They were not the first. They had been preceded by their own kind, by men who carried the same emblem and perhaps the same hopes, and who had vanished from history so completely that not even a whisper of their existence remained.

"It's a bad sign, that's what it is," muttered a hulking miner named Davies, his knuckles white as he gripped the haft of his pickaxe. "They came, and they ain't here now. That ought to tell us somethin'. I say we take what we can from this outer chamber and be on our way. There's ill luck in that dark passage."

A murmur of agreement rippled through the assembled men. The sight of the glittering metal in the sluices was a fresh and potent memory, but the ancient, inexplicable crest on the wall was a present and powerful omen.

"Nonsense!" boomed Professor Croft, turning to face them, his eyes blazing with a fire that seemed to hold the encroaching darkness at bay. "Ill luck? We make our own luck, my friends! We are men of science and industry, not superstitious peasants frightened of shadows! That symbol is not a curse; it is a challenge! It tells us that we are on the right path, that the treasure within is so great that others have sought it before us. Shall we be undone by their failure? Or shall we succeed where they vanished? Think of the glory! Think of the story we will have to tell!"

He gestured towards the dark opening they had made. "We have breached the wall. We are standing on the very threshold of the discovery of a lifetime. Are you so willing to turn your backs on it now? To return to London with your wages and a tale of how you were frightened away by a carving on a rock?" He let the question hang in the air, a direct challenge to their pride and their courage. "I am going in," he declared, his voice ringing with conviction. "I must know what lies beyond. I must solve this riddle. Any man who values his life more than this great adventure is free to remain here. But those who would share in the ultimate discovery, and the rewards that come with it, will follow me now!"

He did not wait for an answer but snatched a lantern from a nearby crate and strode purposefully towards the breach. Thomas, his face pale but his eyes resolute, was instantly at his side. For a moment, the other men hesitated, a knot of uncertain figures caught between fear and ambition. Then Grimes, with a gruff laugh, broke the spell. The lure of treasure, combined with the shame of being thought a coward, was a potent motivator. The passage was not a natural cave but a man-made corridor, its walls constructed of massive, seamlessly fitted stone blocks that dwarfed anything they had seen in the ruins above. The air was cool and still, carrying the scent of dry dust and ages past. Their footsteps, which had been boisterous and confident outside, were now soft and shuffling, as if they were walking in a great cathedral. The silence was profound, broken only by the drip of unseen water and the soft hiss of their lanterns.

They walked for what seemed an eternity, the corridor sloping gently downwards into the bowels of the earth. The passage twisted and turned, but always the workmanship remained the same: precise, masterful, and utterly alien. Finally, it opened into a cavern so vast that the light of their collected lanterns was swallowed by the immensity of it. The ceiling was lost in the gloom far above, and the far walls were shrouded in shadow.

But it was the centre of the room that drew every eye and stopped every heart. There, upon a dais of polished stone, rested a collection of objects that glittered and shone in the lantern light. It was a hoard of treasure beyond their wildest dreams.
